claim: The 4.5 Å structure of the ~2.2 MDa pore complex of pneumolysin was determined by cryoEM.
source: We have determined the 4.5 Å structure of the ~2.2 MDa pore complex of pneumolysin, the main virulence factor of Streptococcus pneumoniae, by cryoEM.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution, molecular weight, and method used for structure determination.

claim: Pneumolysin is the main virulence factor of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source: We have determined the 4.5 Å structure of the ~2.2 MDa pore complex of pneumolysin, the main virulence factor of Streptococcus pneumoniae, by cryoEM.
evidence: The manuscript directly states that pneumolysin is the main virulence factor of S. pneumoniae.

claim: The pneumolysin pore is a 400 Å ring of 42 membrane-inserted monomers.
source: The pneumolysin pore is a 400 Å ring of 42 membrane-inserted monomers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the diameter and number of monomers in the pore complex.

claim: Domain 3 of the soluble toxin refolds into two ~85 Å β-hairpins that traverse the lipid bilayer.
source: Domain 3 of the soluble toxin refolds into two ~85 Å β-hairpins that traverse the lipid bilayer and assemble into a 168-strand β-barrel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the refolding of Domain 3 and the dimensions of the β-hairpins.

claim: The β-hairpins assemble into a 168-strand β-barrel.
source: Domain 3 of the soluble toxin refolds into two ~85 Å β-hairpins that traverse the lipid bilayer and assemble into a 168-strand β-barrel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of strands in the β-barrel formed by the β-hairpins.

claim: The pore complex is stabilized by salt bridges between β-hairpins of adjacent subunits.
source: The pore complex is stabilized by salt bridges between β-hairpins of adjacent subunits and an internal α-barrel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that salt bridges between adjacent subunits contribute to pore stability.

claim: The pore complex is stabilized by an internal α-barrel.
source: The pore complex is stabilized by salt bridges between β-hairpins of adjacent subunits and an internal α-barrel.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that an internal α-barrel contributes to pore stability.

claim: The apolar outer barrel surface with large sidechains is immersed in the lipid bilayer.
source: The apolar outer barrel surface with large sidechains is immersed in the lipid bilayer, while the inner barrel surface is highly charged.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the hydrophobic nature of the outer barrel surface and its interaction with the lipid bilayer.

claim: The inner barrel surface is highly charged.
source: The apolar outer barrel surface with large sidechains is immersed in the lipid bilayer, while the inner barrel surface is highly charged.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the inner surface of the barrel is highly charged.

claim: Gram-positive bacteria utilize cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs) to attack and kill mammalian and human cells.
source: Gram-positive bacteria, including the common wound-infecting Staphylococcus aureus, the virulent food-borne pathogen Listeria monocytogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae that causes pneumonia, utilize cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (CDCs) to attack and kill mammalian and human cells (Gilbert, 2005; Tweten, 2005).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that Gram-positive bacteria use CDCs to attack cells, supported by citations.

claim: CDCs assemble into large, 200–500 Å cytolytic pores on cholesterol-containing cell membranes.
source: The bacteria produce and release CDCs as water-soluble monomers that attach to cholesterol-containing cell membranes, where they assemble into large, 200–500 Å cytolytic pores (Olofsson et al., 1993).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the size range of CDC pores, supported by a citation.

claim: X-ray structures of pneumolysin show that the soluble toxin monomers are roughly rod-shaped and consist of four domains (D1-D4).
source: X-ray structures of pneumolysin (PLY) from S. pneumoniae (Lawrence et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2015; van Pee et al., 2016) show that the soluble toxin monomers are roughly rod-shaped and consist of four domains (D1-D4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the shape and domain structure of PLY monomers, supported by citations to X-ray structures.

claim: All CDCs have the same domain structure and insert into target membranes in essentially the same way.
source: Sequence comparison suggests that all CDCs have the same domain structure and therefore insert into target membranes in essentially the same way (Tweten et al., 2001).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that sequence comparison suggests a conserved mechanism, supported by a citation.

claim: The size heterogeneity of CDC prepores and pores has precluded structure determination at high resolution.
source: The size heterogeneity of CDC prepores and pores has so far precluded structure determination at high resolution.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that size heterogeneity has been a barrier to high-resolution structure determination.

claim: Pore complexes of wildtype PLY forming on unilamellar, cholesterol-containing liposomes were solubilized with detergent.
source: Ring-shaped pore complexes of wildtype PLY (PLYWT) forming on unilamellar, cholesterol-containing liposomes were solubilized with detergent.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental procedure for preparing pore complexes.

claim: The size and homogeneity of solubilized PLY pores is detergent-dependent.
source: The size and homogeneity of solubilized PLY pores is detergent-dependent, as indicated by negative-stain and cryoEM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that detergent affects pore size and homogeneity, with reference to a figure showing this.

claim: Pore diameters varied from 310 to 500 Å in DDM or 350 to 400 Å in Cymal-6.
source: Pore diameters varied from 310 to 500 Å in DDM or 350 to 400 Å in Cymal-6.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides measurements of pore diameters in different detergents.

claim: Replacing the detergent Cymal-6 by amphipol A8-35 resulted in a stable population that was sufficiently homogenous for single-particle cryoEM.
source: Replacing the detergent Cymal-6 by amphipol A8-35 (Althoff et al., 2011; Lu et al., 2014) resulted in a stable population that was sufficiently homogenous for single-particle cryoEM.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that amphipol A8-35 improved sample homogeneity for cryoEM, with supporting citations.

claim: Pore complexes were rings of 42 subunits with an aggregate molecular mass of 2.2 MDa.
source: Pore complexes were rings of 42 subunits with an aggregate molecular mass of 2.2 MDa.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of subunits and molecular mass of the pore complex.

claim: 6461 ring images were combined to generate a 3D map with 42-fold symmetry at 4.5 Å resolution.
source: In total, 6461 ring images were combined to generate a 3D map with 42-fold symmetry at 4.5 Å resolution (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplements 2B and 3,).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of images used and the resolution achieved, with reference to figures.

claim: The final map of the pore complex has an outer diameter of 400 Å and a total height of 110 Å.
source: The final map of the pore complex has an outer diameter of 400 Å and a total height of 110 Å, of which ~80 Å protrudes from the membrane surface (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides dimensions of the pore complex, with reference to a figure.

claim: ~80 Å of the pore complex protrudes from the membrane surface.
source: The final map of the pore complex has an outer diameter of 400 Å and a total height of 110 Å, of which ~80 Å protrudes from the membrane surface (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the height of the pore complex above the membrane, with reference to a figure.

claim: Individual domains of the PLY x-ray structure were moved manually into the 4.5 Å cryoEM map as rigid bodies.
source: Where possible, individual domains of the PLY x-ray structure (van Pee et al., 2016) were moved manually into the 4.5 Å cryoEM map as rigid bodies.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the model building procedure.

claim: Comparison to the soluble form revealed a complete reorganization of the toxin upon membrane insertion.
source: Comparison to the soluble form (Figure 2A,B) revealed a complete reorganization of the toxin upon membrane insertion.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the toxin undergoes complete reorganization, with reference to figures.

claim: D1 and D4 fitted the map of the pore complex with minimal modifications.
source: Of the four protein domains D1-D4 in the x-ray structure, D1 and D4 fitted the map of the pore complex with minimal modifications (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that D1 and D4 required minimal changes, with reference to figures and video.

claim: In the membrane-inserted form, the loop linking D1 to D2 refolds into a helix (α3a).
source: In the membrane-inserted form, the loop linking D1 to D2 refolds into a helix (α3a) at the interface between the rearranged domains D1, D2 and D3 (Figures 2A,E, 3 and 4; Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the refolding of the D1-D2 linker, with reference to multiple figures.

claim: The highly conserved undecapeptide loop renders PLY cholesterol-specific.
source: In D4, the highly conserved undecapeptide loop (Figure 3) that renders PLY cholesterol-specific (Soltani et al., 2007b) was shifted by up to ~9 Å into the cryoEM map (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the function of the undecapeptide loop, supported by a citation.

claim: The undecapeptide loop was shifted by up to ~9 Å into the cryoEM map.
source: In D4, the highly conserved undecapeptide loop (Figure 3) that renders PLY cholesterol-specific (Soltani et al., 2007b) was shifted by up to ~9 Å into the cryoEM map (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the magnitude of the shift observed in the undecapeptide loop.

claim: The undecapeptide loops of adjacent protomers in the pore complex are located in one plane on the outer membrane surface of the target cell.
source: The undecapeptide loops of adjacent protomers in the pore complex are located in one plane on the outer membrane surface of the target cell, where they interact closely with the lipid head groups (Figures 1B and 2A,C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the spatial arrangement of the undecapeptide loops, with reference to figures.

claim: In the linear rows of soluble PLY monomers, the distance between the loops of neighbouring monomers is ~14 Å.
source: In the linear rows of soluble PLY monomers that are found in the PLY crystal structures (Lawrence et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2015; van Pee et al., 2016), the distance between the loops of neighbouring monomers is ~14 Å.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the distance measurement in the crystal structure, with supporting citations.

claim: In the pore complex, the distance between the loops of neighbouring monomers decreases to 4–5 Å.
source: In the pore complex this distance decreases to 4–5 Å, which enables an interaction of the loop that connects β-strands 18 and 19 (β18/19) in D4 with the β22/23 loop in D4 of the next monomer along the ring (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the distance measurement in the pore complex, with reference to figures and video.

claim: The close proximity of loop β18/19 to the undecapeptide of the adjacent monomer suggests a critical role of these D4 loops in receptor recognition and oligomer formation.
source: The close proximity of loop β18/19 that contains Asp403, Thr405, and His407 of one monomer to loop β18/19 and the uncedapeptide containing Trp433 of the adjacent monomer suggests a critical role of these D4 loops not only in receptor recognition, but also in oligomer formation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests a functional role based on structural observations.

claim: Domains 2 and 3 undergo massive rearrangement and refolding in the membrane-inserted form.
source: Domains 2 and 3 undergo massive rearrangement and refolding (Figure 2A,B) in the membrane-inserted form.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that D2 and D3 undergo major structural changes, with reference to figures.

claim: The elongated two-stranded β-sheet of D2 rotates by 90° around a short glycine linker to an orientation parallel to the membrane plane in the pore complex.
source: The elongated two-stranded β-sheet of D2 rotates from its vertical position in the x-ray structure by 90° around a short glycine linker to an orientation parallel to the membrane plane in the pore complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the rotation of D2 and its orientation change.

claim: D2 rotation results in a roughly linear translation of D1 by 35 Å towards the membrane surface and by 30 Å towards the pore centre.
source: D2 connects D1 to D4, and its rotation results in a roughly linear translation of D1 by 35 Å towards the membrane surface and by 30 Å towards the pore centre.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides measurements of D1 movement resulting from D2 rotation.

claim: In the soluble toxin, the central, five-stranded β-sheet in D3 is flanked by two bundles of short α-helices.
source: In the soluble toxin, the central, five-stranded β-sheet in D3 is flanked by two bundles of short α-helices (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structure of D3 in the soluble form, with reference to a figure.

claim: In the pore complex, both helix bundles in D3 refold into four 85 Å β-strands, which form two parallel β-hairpins that insert into and traverse the lipid bilayer.
source: In the pore complex, both bundles refold into four 85 Å β-strands, which form two parallel β-hairpins that insert into and traverse the lipid bilayer (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the refolding of helix bundles into β-hairpins, with reference to a figure.

claim: The β-hairpins of neighbouring subunits coalesce into one extensive, 168-strand β-barrel with an inner diameter of 260 Å.
source: The β-hairpins of neighbouring subunits coalesce into one extensive, 168-strand β-barrel with an inner diameter of 260 Å (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the assembly of β-hairpins into a β-barrel and provides its dimensions, with reference to a figure.

claim: The two new, long β-hairpins are inclined by 20° relative to the membrane normal.
source: The two new, long β-hairpins are inclined by 20° relative to the membrane normal, in good agreement with predictions for perfringolysin O on the basis of cysteine crosslinking experiments (Sato et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the angle of inclination and compares it to predictions from another study, with a citation.

claim: Five of the six helices in bundles HB1 and HB2 refold into β-strands in the pore complex, while one remains intact.
source: While five of the six helices in bundles HB1 and HB2 refold into β-strands in the pore complex, one remains intact.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which helices refold and which remain intact.

claim: The loop and fifth β-strand in the central β-sheet of D3 refold into a helix.
source: Conversely, the loop and fifth β-strand in the central β-sheet of D3 refold into a helix (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the refolding of a β-strand into a helix, with reference to figures.

claim: The two α-helices form a helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif.
source: Together, the two α-helices form a helix-turn-helix (HTH) motif (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the formation of an HTH motif, with reference to a figure.

claim: The HTH motifs of the 42 subunits line up in one plane on the exoplasmic side of the molecule and form an α-barrel inside the β-barrel.
source: In the ring, the HTH motifs of the 42 subunits line up in one plane on the exoplasmic side of the molecule and form an α-barrel inside the β-barrel (Figures 1B and 4), restricting the pore diameter locally to 250 Å (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the arrangement of HTH motifs and their effect on pore diameter, with reference to figures.

claim: The HTH motifs restrict the pore diameter locally to 250 Å.
source: In the ring, the HTH motifs of the 42 subunits line up in one plane on the exoplasmic side of the molecule and form an α-barrel inside the β-barrel (Figures 1B and 4), restricting the pore diameter locally to 250 Å (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the local pore diameter at the HTH motifs, with reference to a figure.

claim: The outside of the membrane-inserted part of the β-barrel is almost entirely hydrophobic.
source: The outside of the membrane-inserted part of the β-barrel is almost entirely hydrophobic (Figure 5A,E) and covered by the toroid density of disordered amphipol that replaces the membrane lipid (Figure 1B), as in the cryoEM structures of amphipol-solubilized membrane proteins (Althoff et al., 2011; Liao et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the hydrophobic nature of the outer barrel surface, with reference to figures and supporting citations.

claim: The inside pore surface is highly polar, with three aspartates and two glutamates forming a 15 by 9 Å patch of negative charge.
source: The inside pore surface is highly polar, with three aspartates and two glutamates forming a 15 by 9 Å patch of negative charge, flanked above and below by positive charges (Figure 5B,F,G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the charge distribution on the inner pore surface, with reference to figures.

claim: Three factors contribute to pore stability: surface and charge complementarity of the membrane-inserted monomers, alternating positive and negative charges of helices α13a and α13b in the α-barrel, and ionic interactions between charged sidechains in adjacent β-strands of the pore barrel.
source: Apart from the hydrogen bonds between the 168 β-strands in the barrel and the interactions of helix α3a with D1 and β-hairpin one (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), three other factors contribute to pore stability: (1) the surface and charge complementarity of the membrane-inserted monomers (Figure 5C); (2) the alternating positive and negative charges of helices α13a and α13b in the α-barrel (Figure 5D); and (3) ionic interactions between charged sidechains in adjacent β-strands of the pore barrel (Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists three factors contributing to pore stability, with reference to figures.

claim: Asp168 and Glu170 in β-strand β7 are in a good position for forming a salt bridge with Lys271 in β-strand β10 of the next-door monomer.
source: In particular, Asp168 and Glu170 in β-strand β7 are in a good position for forming a salt bridge with Lys271 in β-strand β10 of the next-door monomer (Figure 5G).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes potential salt bridge formation between specific residues, with reference to a figure.

claim: Liposomes were studded with numerous ring-shaped complexes of 290 to 360 Å outer diameter.
source: The liposomes were studded with numerous ring-shaped complexes of 290 to 360 Å outer diameter (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the size range of ring-shaped complexes observed on liposomes, with reference to a figure.

claim: Assemblies were identified as PLY pores or prepores by the absence or presence of a lipid bilayer within the ring.
source: Assemblies were identified as PLY pores or prepores by the absence or presence of a lipid bilayer within the ring (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the criterion for distinguishing pores from prepores, with reference to a figure.

claim: The subtomogram average map of the prepore complex at a resolution of 22 Å had an outer diameter of 320 Å and accommodated 34 subunits.
source: The subtomogram average map of the prepore complex at a resolution of 22 Å (Figure 6C) had an outer diameter of 320 Å and accommodated 34 subunits (Figure 6D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the resolution, diameter, and number of subunits in the prepore complex, with reference to figures.

claim: The model 5cr6 fitted the prepore map best, indicating that in this structure the soluble toxin is in the pre-pore state.
source: Of the available PLY crystal structures (Lawrence et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2015; van Pee et al., 2016), the model 5cr6 (Marshall et al., 2015) fitted the map best (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that in this structure the soluble toxin is in the pre-pore state.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which crystal structure fits the prepore map best and interprets this as representing the pre-pore state, with citations and reference to a figure.

claim: The subtomogram average map of the pore complex at 27 Å resolution indicated a slightly larger diameter of around 350 Å and consisted of 34 subunits.
source: The subtomogram average map of the pore complex at 27 Å resolution (Figure 6C) indicated a slightly larger diameter of around 350 Å, but likewise consisted of 34 subunits (Figure 6E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the resolution, diameter, and number of subunits in the pore complex from subtomogram averaging, with reference to figures.

claim: The model of membrane-inserted PLY fitted the subtomogram average of the pore complex without significant adjustment, including the 20° inclination of the long β-hairpins relative to the membrane normal.
source: The model of membrane-inserted PLY fitted the subtomogram average of the pore complex without significant adjustment, including the 20° inclination of the long β-hairpins relative to the membrane normal.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that the model fits the subtomogram average well, confirming the β-hairpin inclination.

claim: AFM revealed two different forms of PLY prepores in planar bilayers, rising 110 or 80 Å above the membrane surface.
source: Atomic force microscopy (AFM) had revealed two different forms of PLY prepores in planar bilayers, rising 110 or 80 Å above the membrane surface (van Pee et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes two prepore forms observed by AFM, with a citation.

claim: The low prepore form has the same height as the pore complex, but the lipid bilayer is still intact.
source: The low form has the same height as the pore complex, but the lipid bilayer is still intact.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the characteristics of the low prepore form.

claim: In the lower prepore, D1, D2 and D4 have moved to their positions in the pore assembly, while D3 has not yet refolded and the long, membrane-spanning β-hairpins have not yet formed.
source: We propose that in this lower prepore, D1, D2 and D4 have moved to their positions in the pore assembly, while D3 has not yet refolded and the long, membrane-spanning β-hairpins have not yet formed.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes a structural model for the lower prepore state.

claim: The tall prepore form is assigned to an early prepore state, which then rearranges into the lower, late prepore state.
source: We assign the tall form to an early prepore state, which then rearranges into the lower, late prepore state.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly assigns the tall prepore form to an early state in the pore formation pathway.

claim: The early prepore is essentially a ring-shaped side-by-side arrangement of soluble PLY monomers.
source: The cross-section profile (Figure 6B,D) shows that the early prepore is essentially a ring-shaped side-by-side arrangement of soluble PLY monomers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), similar to that in the crystal lattice (Lawrence et al., 2015; Marshall et al., 2015; van Pee et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structure of the early prepore, with reference to figures and citations.

claim: The late prepore was observed for 13% of the rings on planar bilayers examined by AFM.
source: While the late prepore was observed for 13% of the rings on planar bilayers examined by AFM, it was not observed in tomographic volumes of PLY on liposomes, implying that it is an intermediate, transient state which inserts more readily into curved liposomes than into planar bilayers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the percentage of late prepores observed by AFM.

claim: The late prepore is an intermediate, transient state which inserts more readily into curved liposomes than into planar bilayers.
source: While the late prepore was observed for 13% of the rings on planar bilayers examined by AFM, it was not observed in tomographic volumes of PLY on liposomes, implying that it is an intermediate, transient state which inserts more readily into curved liposomes than into planar bilayers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly infers that the late prepore is transient and membrane curvature-dependent based on observations.

claim: Prepore stability and membrane insertion are related to membrane curvature, such that pores form preferentially in lipid bilayers with a convex curvature.
source: Prepore stability and membrane insertion thus seem to be related to membrane curvature, such that pores form preferentially in lipid bilayers with a convex curvature.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes a relationship between membrane curvature and pore formation.

claim: X-ray data were collected to 2.45 and 2.5 Å resolution from crystals of PLYD168A and PLYΔ146/147.
source: X-ray data were collected to 2.45 and 2.5 Å resolution from crystals of PLYD168A and PLYΔ146/147 (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the resolution of X-ray data collected for the mutants, with reference to a table.

claim: Superposition of both mutant structures on PLYWT showed no significant overall differences.
source: Superposition of both structures on PLYWT showed no significant overall differences, although a detailed comparison indicated small changes in domain D2, helix bundle HB2 and in two of the D4 loops (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that overall structures are similar but with minor local differences, with reference to a figure.

claim: The deletion of Ala146 and Arg147 caused significant conformational changes in the loop connecting helix α5 to strand β7 of the central β-sheet.
source: Around the mutated residue in PLYD168A differences were restricted to sidechain orientations, while the deletion of two residues in PLYΔ146/147 caused significant conformational changes in the loop connecting helix α5 to strand β7 of the central β-sheet.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the structural consequences of the deletion mutation.

claim: The deletion of Ala146 and Arg147 caused a slight shift of helix α5 towards D3.
source: This deletion also caused a slight shift of helix α5 towards D3 (Figure 8).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes a structural change caused by the deletion, with reference to a figure.

claim: PLYD168A bound to cholesterol-containing liposomes and oligomerized into rings.
source: Like PLYWT, PLYD168A bound to cholesterol-containing liposomes and oligomerized into rings (Figure 7A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the behavior of the PLYD168A mutant, with reference to a figure.

claim: Unlike PLYWT that lysed the liposomes within a short time, liposomes incubated with PLYD168A remained intact for hours.
source: However, unlike PLYWT that lysed the liposomes within a short time, liposomes incubated with PLYD168A remained intact for hours.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the lytic activity of PLYD168A to wildtype.

claim: The rings of PLYD168A frequently detached from the liposomes, indicating they were prepores that had not yet inserted into the membrane.
source: Frequently, the rings detached from the liposomes, indicating they were prepores that had not yet inserted into the membrane.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the detachment of rings as evidence that they are prepores.

claim: The hemolytic activity of PLYD168A was reduced by 80% compared to PLYWT.
source: This is also reflected by the hemolytic activity, which was reduced by 80% compared to PLYWT, highlighting the important role of Asp168 in ionic interactions between β-strands that stabilize the pore complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the percentage reduction in hemolytic activity for PLYD168A.

claim: Asp168 plays an important role in ionic interactions between β-strands that stabilize the pore complex.
source: This is also reflected by the hemolytic activity, which was reduced by 80% compared to PLYWT, highlighting the important role of Asp168 in ionic interactions between β-strands that stabilize the pore complex.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly interprets the functional data to infer the role of Asp168.

claim: PLYΔ146/147 was not able to bind to the membranes at all and had no detectable hemolytic activity.
source: PLYΔ146/147 was not able to bind to the membranes at all and had no detectable hemolytic activity (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the complete loss of function in the PLYΔ146/147 mutant, with reference to a figure.

claim: Ionic interactions between the β-strands contribute significantly to pore stability.
source: Ionic interactions between the β-strands thus contribute significantly to pore stability, and any disruption of these interactions compromises pore formation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly concludes that ionic interactions are important for pore stability based on mutational data.

claim: Any disruption of ionic interactions between β-strands compromises pore formation.
source: Ionic interactions between the β-strands thus contribute significantly to pore stability, and any disruption of these interactions compromises pore formation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that disrupting ionic interactions affects pore formation.

claim: The mutations pinpoint protein regions that are promising targets for drug development.
source: Both mutations pinpoint protein regions that are promising targets for drug development.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly suggests that the mutated regions could be drug targets.

claim: Drugs that interfere with ionic interactions between β-strands would render the toxin ineffective.
source: Drugs that interfere with these interactions would render the toxin ineffective, and the bacteria that produce it non-pathogenic.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes that drugs targeting these interactions could neutralize the toxin.

claim: The number of monomers in the ring varies from one liposome preparation to another, or the rings rearrange into a more stable form upon detergent solubilisation.
source: This means that either the number of subunits in the ring varies from one liposome preparation to another, or that the rings rearrange into a more stable form upon detergent solubilisation, which we consider more likely.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes two possible explanations for the difference in subunit number, favoring one.

claim: An earlier, low-resolution cryoEM structure of PLY pores and prepores deduced that there were 31 ± 3 subunits in the prepore and 38 or 44 in the pore complex.
source: Interestingly, an earlier, low-resolution cryoEM structure of PLY pores and prepores in lipid bilayers deduced that there were 31 ± 3 subunits in the prepore and 38 or 44 in the pore complex (Tilley et al., 2005), in good agreement with our findings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly cites earlier work and compares it to current findings.

claim: The rings can grow in the membrane by incorporating further subunits.
source: Since the PLY pores in our subtomogram averages were smaller, consisting of 34 rather than 42 subunits, it seems that the rings can grow in the membrane by incorporating further subunits.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes that rings can grow by adding subunits based on observed size differences.

claim: Complexes of 42 monomers are more stable than both larger and smaller rings.
source: Apparently, complexes of 42 monomers are more stable than both larger and smaller rings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly proposes that 42-subunit rings are most stable.

claim: Earlier cryoEM work, AFM and FRET studies have described the vertical height change of the prepore upon membrane insertion in terms of a collapse or unfolding of D2.
source: Earlier cryoEM work, AFM and FRET studies have described the vertical height change of the prepore upon membrane insertion in terms of a collapse or unfolding of D2 (Czajkowsky et al., 2004; Ramachandran et al., 2005; Tilley et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly cites earlier work describing D2 changes, with citations.

claim: The atomic model of the pore complex shows that the height change is due to a rigid-body rotation of D2, in which the structure of the domain remains intact.
source: Our atomic model of the pore complex now shows that this change is due to a rigid-body rotation of D2, in which the structure of the domain remains intact.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly corrects earlier interpretations based on the new atomic model.

claim: Time-lapse AFM of PLY and listeriolysin (LLO) on planar membranes indicated that the vertical height change is not directly linked to pore formation.
source: Time-lapse AFM of PLY and listeriolysin (LLO) on planar membranes indicated that the vertical height change is not directly linked to pore formation (Mulvihill et al., 2015; van Pee et al., 2016), in line with a mechanism that involves two different prepore states that we refer to as the early and late prepore.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly cites AFM studies showing that height change and pore formation are not directly linked, with citations.

claim: The 5-stranded central β-sheet in the crystal structure of D3 fits into the cryoET map of the early prepore complex without any modification.
source: The 5-stranded central β-sheet in the crystal structure of D3 fits into the cryoET map of the early prepore complex without any modification, but the late prepore model indicates a potential steric clash between the short β-strand in the central β-sheet of D3 and the adjacent monomer.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes how the crystal structure fits the early prepore map.

claim: The late prepore model indicates a potential steric clash between the short β-strand in the central β-sheet of D3 and the adjacent monomer.
source: The 5-stranded central β-sheet in the crystal structure of D3 fits into the cryoET map of the early prepore complex without any modification, but the late prepore model indicates a potential steric clash between the short β-strand in the central β-sheet of D3 and the adjacent monomer.
